item.title: Sound Made From Typing?! A Hundred Years of Electroacoustic Music
item.description:
Can sound really be made just by typing?
From a French engineer splicing tape in 1948 to AI models generating a full arrangement in real time today, the last hundred years of electroacoustic music are really the story of humanity continuously redefining what counts as music. In three minutes, Little Pi walks you through the key turning points: musique concrète, electronic music, programmable composition tools, and today's generative AI.

item.title: She Drew Sound Onto Film: Oramics Inventor Daphne Oram
item.description:
Someone figured out how to draw sound long before graphic design software even existed. Little Pi introduces British electronic music pioneer Daphne Oram, who co-founded the BBC's Radiophonic Workshop, then resigned less than a year later to build Oramics: a machine that turned hand-drawn waveforms on strips of film into sound, an idea that conceptually foreshadowed the automation curves in today's music production software.

item.title: What Is Sample Rate? The Strange Number Behind CD Audio Quality
item.description:
First episode of a new mini-series on everyday audio-tech trivia. CD audio quality is always labeled 44100, an oddly specific number. item.title: He Cranked a Vibrato Too Far and Invented the Sound of the 80s: John Chowning and FM Synthesis
item.description:
Stanford professor John Chowning was experimenting with vibrato in 1967 and pushed the wobble speed far past any normal range, accidentally discovering FM synthesis. Yamaha later licensed the technology to build the DX7, which defined the sound of 1980s pop music. In February 2026, Chowning finally received a Technical Grammy Award for the discovery.

item.title: What Is MIDI, Really? Not a Recording, an Instruction Sheet
item.description:
A MIDI file doesn't actually contain any recorded sound? Little Pi explains the core difference between MIDI and MP3 or WAV: it doesn't store a waveform, it stores a detailed performance instruction sheet. From the 1983 standard that let synthesizers from different brands talk to each other, to why MIDI files are so tiny and can switch instruments instantly, to why it's still used everywhere from game scores to AI music tools over forty years later.

item.title: How Does a Synth Actually "Sculpt" Sound? Subtractive Synthesis and the ADSR Envelope
item.description:
Following up on MIDI, Little Pi explains how a synthesizer actually makes a sound: an oscillator generates a raw, overtone-rich, harsh waveform, a filter carves away the unwanted frequencies, and the ADSR envelope (attack, decay, sustain, release) gives the sound its personality. Tweak the envelope on the exact same waveform and you can go from a drum hit to a lush string-like pad - a logic that applies to nearly every synthesizer out there.
References: Subtractive synthesis - Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subtractive_synthesis Envelope (music) - Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envelope_(music)

item.title: Writing Music with a Computer for the First Time! Max Mathews, Father of Computer Music
item.description:
In this episode, Little Pi introduces Max Mathews, honored as the "father of computer music." An electrical engineer at Bell Labs, he wrote MUSIC, the first computer music program, on an IBM 704 mainframe in 1957. In 1961 his colleagues had a computer sing "Daisy Bell" with a synthesized voice, a demo that later inspired the scene where HAL 9000 sings in "2001: A Space Odyssey." His "unit generator" building-block design shaped Csound, SuperCollider, ChucK, and nearly every music programming language since.
References: Max Mathews - Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Max_Mathews MUSIC-N - Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MUSIC-N Daisy Bell - Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daisy_Bell Csound official website: https://csound.com/

item.title: Twist a Knob, Press a Pedal: What Is MIDI CC?
item.description:
Turn a knob, push a fader, or press a pedal on a MIDI keyboard, and the sound in your computer changes. The hero behind it is MIDI CC (Control Change). In this episode, Little Pi explains what's inside a CC message: a controller number plus a value, both ranging from 0 to 127. Meet the most common numbers: 1 for the modulation wheel, 7 for volume, 10 for pan, 11 for expression, and 64 for the sustain pedal. Finally, learn how drawing CC curves in your music software creates automation.

item.title: Why Do All Songs Sound Equally Loud on Streaming? What Is LUFS?
item.description:
Why do songs on streaming platforms all sound about equally loud, one after another? Little Pi starts with the loudness war, then introduces LUFS, the loudness unit defined by the ITU-R BS.1770 standard that imitates how human ears hear. LUFS numbers are usually negative, and closer to zero means louder: the EBU R128 broadcast recommendation targets minus 23 LUFS, while Spotify plays back at around minus 14 LUFS by default. Finally, learn how loudness normalization works, why over-squashed masters lose out, and why you should leave headroom for peaks in your own music.

item.description:

item.description:
The 1956 sci-fi film Forbidden Planet has a score with no traditional orchestra at all, only electronic sounds, created by the married couple Bebe and Louis Barron. item.title: Why Do You Sound Better in the Shower? Reverb Explained
item.description:
Why do you sound like a star when you sing in the shower? The answer is reverb. In this audio tip, Little Pi explains the difference between reverb and echo; how Harvard physicist Wallace Sabine rescued a lecture hall where words lingered for 5.5 seconds in 1895, defined reverberation time (RT60), and helped design Boston Symphony Hall, which opened in 1900; Bill Putnam turning a women's restroom into an echo chamber in 1947; the roughly 270-kilogram EMT 140 plate reverb of 1957; the EMT 250, the first commercial digital reverb, in 1976; and convolution reverb, which captures a real space with an impulse response. Plus a mixing tip: more reverb isn't always better!

item.title: Can You Retouch Sound? The Equalizer (EQ) Explained
item.description:

item.title: The Singing Building: The 1958 Philips Pavilion and Varèse's Poème électronique
item.description:
At the 1958 Brussels World's Fair, there was a building with hundreds of loudspeakers hidden in its walls, and it sang when you walked in! In this episode, Little Pi introduces the Philips Pavilion: commissioned by the electronics company Philips from architect Le Corbusier, who wanted not a showroom but an "electronic poem"; designed by Iannis Xenakis, also a composer, from nine hyperbolic paraboloids; and filled with Edgard Varèse's Poème électronique. Varèse, who championed "organized sound" and wrote the all-percussion Ionisation in 1931, created the roughly eight-minute piece from September 1957 to April 1958. Played from three tape tracks, it was routed with telephone dials through three to four hundred wall-mounted speakers, moving around the audience: one of the earliest immersive sound systems. The pavilion was demolished on January 30, 1959, and was later rebuilt virtually in an EU-funded project.

item.title: The Box That Keeps Sound Steady: What Is a Compressor?
item.description:

item.title: Bach on a Synthesizer! Wendy Carlos and Switched-On Bach
item.description:
In 1968, an album of Bach played on a synthesizer won three Grammy Awards! Little Pi introduces Wendy Carlos, who studied physics and music at Brown University and earned a master's in composition from Columbia in 1965. She met Robert Moog in 1964 and convinced him to add a touch-sensitive keyboard. Because the synthesizer could only play one note at a time, Switched-On Bach was built up layer by layer on an eight-track recorder over about 1,100 hours, and it topped the classical albums chart for three years. She went on to score A Clockwork Orange, The Shining and Tron, divided the octave into 35 notes on Beauty in the Beast in 1986, and received the SEAMUS Lifetime Achievement Award in 2005.

item.title: Make a Synthesizer Talk! What Is a Vocoder?
item.description:
That robot singing in electronic songs is really a human voice controlling a synthesizer! Little Pi introduces the vocoder: Homer Dudley at Bell Labs patented it in 1938 to compress speech and save telephone bandwidth. It splits the voice into frequency bands and uses each band's loudness to control a synthesizer. In World War Two it became the heart of SIGSALY, the Allies' encrypted phone system (in use from 1943, weighing over 50 tonnes). In 1970 Wendy Carlos and Robert Moog built a ten-band vocoder for the 1971 film A Clockwork Orange, and Kraftwerk's Autobahn (1974) carried it into pop, dance music and hip-hop. Plus: how a vocoder differs from a talk box and Auto-Tune. Try it yourself with EVOC 20 PolySynth in Logic Pro.

item.title: The Man Who Turned Noise into Music: Pierre Schaeffer, Father of Musique Concrète
item.description:
Can trains and pots and pans become music? Little Pi introduces Pierre Schaeffer, the father of musique concrète: born in Nancy, France in 1910 and trained as an engineer, he founded the Studio d'Essai at French radio in 1942. On October 5, 1948, the radio broadcast a "concert of noises" premiering his Cinq études de bruits, including the Railway Study. He cut closed grooves into shellac records to loop sounds forever, the ancestor of today's loop. In 1950 he and Pierre Henry created Symphonie pour un homme seul. He founded a musique concrète research group in 1951, reorganized as the GRM in 1958, and introduced the ideas of the sound object and acousmatic listening (hearing a sound without seeing its source). His 1966 Traité des objets musicaux summed up twenty years of research. His students included Éliane Radigue and Jean-Michel Jarre.

item.title: Why Do Some Chords Sound Prickly? The Sensory Dissonance Curve
item.description:
Whether an interval sounds smooth can actually be calculated! Little Pi introduces the sensory dissonance curve: two close frequencies create beats, and faster beats turn into roughness, which Helmholtz proposed in 1863 as the main source of dissonance. In 1965, Plomp and Levelt's listening experiments found that two pure tones sound roughest at about a quarter of a critical band. Add up the roughness between all the overtones of two notes, and the curve's valleys land on the octave, fifth, fourth and major third. William Sethares (1993 paper; 1998 book Tuning, Timbre, Spectrum, Scale) showed that for sounds with uneven overtones, like xylophones, bells and gamelan, the valleys move: timbre and scale are partners, so you can design the timbre first and then the scale.

In 1965, Plomp and Levelt's listening experiments found that two pure tones sound roughest at about a quarter of a critical band. Add up the roughness between all the overtones of two notes, and the curve's valleys land on the octave, fifth, fourth and major third. William Sethares (1993 paper; 1998 book Tuning, Timbre, Spectrum, Scale) showed that for sounds with uneven overtones, like xylophones, bells and gamelan, the valleys move: timbre and scale are partners, so you can design the timbre first and then the scale.

item.title: How Does AI "Read" Sound? Neural Audio Codecs EnCodec and X-Codec
item.description:
Before AI can write a song, it has to learn to read sound! Little Pi introduces neural audio codecs: one second of audio has 24,000 numbers, far too many and too fine, so an encoder squeezes sound into codes and a decoder turns them back into sound. Examples include Google's SoundStream (2021) and Meta's EnCodec (2022, as low as 1.5 kbps). Where do the codes come from? RVQ (residual vector quantization) stacks several codebooks: the first captures the outline, the next fills in the error, layer by layer. X-Codec (2024) adds HuBERT semantic features before the codebooks so the tokens are easier for AI to understand, and the open-source song model YuE uses a compact version of it. These audio tokens are the foundation of music generation models like MusicGen and YuE.

item.title: Is AI Composing Just a Word Chain Game? Autoregressive Generation and MusicGen
item.description:
Is AI composing just a word chain game? Little Pi introduces autoregressive generation: like a phone keyboard guessing your next word, the model looks at all previous audio tokens, guesses the next one, adds it, and guesses again. The Transformer doing the guessing uses attention to look back at earlier rhythms and themes; OpenAI's Jukebox (2020) took this path. Meta's MusicGen, open-sourced in 2023, uses a 32 kHz EnCodec with four codebooks at 50 frames per second, and its delay pattern offsets the codebooks by one step so they can be predicted together, so each second of music takes only 50 steps. It reads text with T5, the melody version can follow a tune you hum, and it was trained on 20,000 hours of licensed music in 300M, 1.5B and 3.3B parameter sizes.

item.title: Carving Music Out of Noise: Diffusion Models and Stable Audio Open
item.description:
Music can be carved out of noise! Little Pi introduces diffusion models: during training, music gets a little more noise at each step, like ink spreading in water, and the AI learns to guess the noise added at each step. To generate, it runs in reverse, starting from pure noise and subtracting noise step by step, guided by a text description. The 2020 DDPM paper made this method a big hit. Riffusion (late 2022) used the image model Stable Diffusion to draw spectrograms, showing that sound can be drawn. Stable Audio Open (2024) denoises in a compressed latent space, using T5 for text and a Transformer for denoising, generating up to 47 seconds of 44.1 kHz stereo audio, trained on about 480,000 Creative Commons licensed recordings from Freesound and the Free Music Archive.

item.title: Does AI Composing Need a Queue? MusicGen's Delay Pattern
item.description:
How should four codebooks take turns? Little Pi takes a deep dive into MusicGen's delay pattern. EnCodec produces 50 frames per second, and with RVQ each frame has four codebooks, so every second has 200 tokens to guess. Pattern one, flattening, guesses one code at a time: most accurate but slowest, 2,000 steps for 10 seconds. Pattern two, parallel, guesses all four codes of a frame at once: only 500 steps, but the layers can't see each other, like coloring before the sketch is done. Pattern three, the delay pattern, starts each codebook one step later, like singing a canon, so finer codebooks can follow the coarse sketch, and 10 seconds takes only 503 steps. The 2023 MusicGen paper compared these patterns: the delay pattern came close to flattening in quality while running almost four times faster, so MusicGen chose it.

item.title: Can Melodies Evolve? Composing with Genetic Algorithms
item.description:
Can melodies evolve? Little Pi introduces the genetic algorithm, which John Holland turned into a computer method in 1975 based on Darwin's survival of the fittest. Start with a random crowd of melodies, where every note is a gene, and score each one (its fitness). Pick high scorers as parents, cut and join their halves (crossover), and once in a while randomly change a note (mutation). Repeat generation after generation, and good-sounding features pile up. Al Biles's GenJam (1994) evolved jazz solos with a human judge and even traded phrases with him on stage, but ran into the fitness bottleneck. DarwinTunes (2012) let 6,931 listeners rate music loops over 2,513 generations, and chords and rhythms emerged from noise. Plus a secret: Teacher Lin Na-Wei's work Salamander Quintet uses a genetic algorithm too.

item.title: Is AI Rolling Dice When It Composes? Temperature, Top-k and Top-p
item.description:
Same prompt, two different songs? Little Pi takes apart the dice behind AI music generation. At every step, an autoregressive model gives a list where every candidate has a probability (each MusicGen codebook has 1,024 candidates). Always picking number one (greedy decoding) is bland and repetitive, so models sample instead. Temperature divides the scores before turning them into probabilities: low is safe, high is risky. Top-k keeps only the top k candidates (MusicGen's default is 250). Top-p, or nucleus sampling (Holtzman et al., 2019), adds probabilities from the top until it passes p, so the number of candidates stretches and shrinks. MusicGen's defaults: temperature 1, top-k 250, top-p 0 (off).

item.title: Why Does AI Follow Your Prompt? Classifier-Free Guidance (CFG) Explained
item.description:
You type "jazz saxophone" and get a piano piece? Little Pi introduces CFG, Classifier-Free Guidance, the knob that makes AI follow your prompt. The older classifier guidance (Dhariwal and Nichol, 2021) needed a separate judge model. In 2021, Jonathan Ho and Tim Salimans had the same model calculate twice at every step, once with the prompt and once without, then amplify the difference (unconditional + scale x (conditional - unconditional)). During training the prompt is randomly dropped: MusicGen drops it 20% of the time, so one model does both jobs. How high to set it: MusicGen defaults to 3 (cfg_coef), and Stable Audio Open's official example uses 7. Too high leaves only one sound and can distort, and calculating twice roughly doubles generation time.

item.title: How Do AI Audio Codebooks Get Clearer Layer by Layer? Residual Vector Quantization (RVQ) Explained
item.description:
Why does AI use several codebooks to turn sound into tokens? Little Pi unpacks RVQ, Residual Vector Quantization, mentioned briefly in episode 36. The encoder cuts sound into short slices, turns each into a vector, and looks up the closest entry in a codebook. One codebook is either too rough or too huge: in the SoundStream paper's example, at 3 kbps and 100 slices per second, a single codebook would need about a billion entries, while 5 codebooks of 64 entries need only 320. In RVQ each codebook only fixes what the previous one left over (the residual), like paying with hundreds, then tens, then ones. EnCodec uses 75 slices per second and 1024 entries per codebook: 2 codebooks = 1.5 kbps, 32 = 24 kbps; MusicGen uses 4 codebooks at 50 slices per second. SoundStream's quantizer dropout randomly uses only the first few codebooks during training, so one model supports multiple quality levels and the first codebook carries the most important information. Multi-stage vector quantization goes back to Juang and Gray's 1982 speech coding work.
References: SoundStream: An End-to-End Neural Audio Codec: https://arxiv.org/abs/2107.03312 SoundStream - Google Research blog: https://research.google/blog/soundstream-an-end-to-end-neural-audio-codec/ High Fidelity Neural Audio Compression (EnCodec): https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.13438 Simple and Controllable Music Generation (MusicGen paper): https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.05284

item.title: How Does AI Know Where to Listen? The Attention Mechanism Explained
item.description:
When AI writes bar nine, how does it know to look back at bar one? Little Pi unpacks the attention mechanism, mentioned briefly in episode 37. Older models worked like a game of telephone, passing information along step by step and forgetting more the farther it went. Attention lets every step look straight back at all earlier steps and give each a score (adding up to 100%): the higher the score, the more attention. How are scores decided? Each step prepares a Query, a Key and a Value; the query is matched against every key, and the better the match, the more of that value gets read, like checking book spines in a library before deciding what to open. Multi-head attention runs several sets at once, each learning its own focus. Music looking at itself is self-attention; looking at text is cross-attention: MusicGen turns the prompt into numbers with T5, then glances back at it with cross-attention. Attention was first used for machine translation in 2014; the 2017 paper Attention Is All You Need gave birth to the Transformer; and in 2018 Google Magenta's Music Transformer wrote minute-long piano music with themes that answer each other. The price: double the steps, four times the comparisons.

item.title: Where Does AI Keep Sound? Latent Space and Autoencoders Explained
item.description:
Episode 38 said Stable Audio Open does diffusion inside a compressed space. Where is that space? Little Pi introduces the latent space and the autoencoder: an encoder squeezes sound down, a decoder rebuilds it, and the narrow bottleneck in the middle only fits the essentials, like packing clothes in vacuum storage bags. The numbers in the bottleneck are like map coordinates, and similar sounds end up close together: flute and oboe are neighbors, drums live in another neighborhood, and the model organizes this by itself. In 2017 Google Magenta's NSynth was trained on about 300,000 single notes; taking the point halfway between a flute and an organ yields a brand-new tone color, later built into the NSynth Super hardware synth. In 2018 MusicVAE morphed gradually between melodies. The 2013 Variational Autoencoder (VAE) turns each sound into a small cloud, so the map has no holes. Stable Audio Open uses a VAE to squeeze 44.1 kHz stereo (88,200 numbers per second) into 21.5 frames per second of 64 numbers each, about 64 times smaller, then runs diffusion on that small map and decodes it back: latent diffusion. Finally, EnCodec (RVQ codes after the bottleneck, for token prediction) versus Stable Audio (continuous coordinates, for diffusion).

item.title: 1000 Steps Is Too Slow! How Diffusion Models Got Faster: Noise Schedules and DDIM
item.description:
Episode 38 said diffusion models wipe noise away step by step until music appears. But how many steps, and how much noise per step? Little Pi explains the noise schedule and sampling steps. The noise schedule is the timetable for adding noise during training, like slowly watering down a glass of juice. In 2020 DDPM used a 1000-step linear schedule, but it adds noise too fast, so a long stretch near the end is pure noise and wasted work. In 2021 OpenAI's Alex Nichol and Prafulla Dhariwal proposed the cosine schedule, slowing down at both ends so every step counts. Generating with 1000 steps is too slow, so Stanford's DDIM (2020) lets the same model take big strides, 10 to 50 times faster in the paper's experiments. item.title: Same Word, Different Jobs! Distillation in Language Models vs Music AI
item.description:
Distillation is a hot word in the language model world, and music generation AI uses it too, but the same word means two different jobs. It comes from a 2015 paper by Geoffrey Hinton and colleagues: a big teacher model guides a small student, giving not just the right answer but soft labels like seventy percent violin, twenty percent viola, using the temperature from episode 41 to make the hints clearer. Language model distillation turns big into small: Hugging Face's DistilBERT (2019) is 40% smaller, 60% faster and keeps about 97% of BERT's language understanding; DeepSeek-R1 (2025) used about 800,000 worked examples to train distilled Qwen and Llama models from 1.5B to 70B. Music diffusion distillation turns many steps into few: progressive distillation (Tim Salimans and Jonathan Ho, Google, 2022) has the student do in one step what the teacher does in two, halving each round from 8192 steps down to 4; then came consistency distillation; and Presto! (Adobe and UC San Diego, 2024) distills both steps and layers, 10 to 18 times faster, 32 seconds of mono music in 0.23 seconds. Finally, a correction: episode 46 said Stable Audio Open Small relies on distillation, but it mainly uses adversarial post-training (ARC), which its authors stress is not distillation.

item.title: No Teacher, Just a Picky Judge! Adversarial Post-Training (ARC) and Stable Audio Open Small
item.description:
Episode 47 corrected that Stable Audio Open Small gets its speed mainly not from distillation but from adversarial post-training (ARC): no teacher model, just a judge whose job is finding faults. The adversarial idea comes from GANs (Ian Goodfellow et al., 2014): a generator like a counterfeiter and a discriminator like a bank inspector. The team first trained a rectified flow model, slimming Stable Audio Open's core from about 1.06 billion to 340 million parameters; it normally needs 50 steps, and post-training coaches it down to 8. Trick one, relativistic adversarial training: a real recording and a generated clip for the same prompt are compared side by side, and the judge says which is more real. Trick two, contrastive training: prompts are shuffled and the judge must catch mismatches, learning to check prompt fit, so the model no longer needs CFG from episode 42 (computing every step twice, with and without the prompt, then amplifying the difference) and computes each step once, saving almost half the memory. Results: 12 seconds of stereo in about 75 ms on an H100, 187 ms on an RTX 3090, about 6.6 s on an Arm phone. In listening tests ARC scored 4.4 for variety versus 2.7 for the distillation method Presto!, at the cost of slightly lower quality and prompt matching. And both papers share the same first author, Zachary Novack.

item.title: Giving AI's Sound Blocks Meaning! X-Codec Semantic Features and Why Fewer Words Go Wrong
item.description:
X-Codec only got one sentence in episode 36, so this episode Little Pi takes it apart. Codecs like EnCodec and DAC were built for compression: they care whether the rebuilt sound sounds the same, not what it means, like a stenographer copying strokes without understanding the words, so models like VALL-E that build speech from audio tokens often skip or misread words. X-Codec brings in HuBERT (Meta, 2021), which learns by hiding part of a clip and guessing it, and so learns to tell what a sound is: semantic features. X-Codec sends sound down two paths, an acoustic encoder for timbre and detail and HuBERT for meaning, merged before the codebook (RVQ); decoding must hand in two assignments, rebuilding the waveform and rebuilding the semantic features. Results with the same VALL-E setup: word error rate 6.37% with EnCodec, 6.81% with DAC, 3.26% with X-Codec, close to 2.23% for real recordings; speech quality score up from 3.02 to 4.22. For music and sound, a general-purpose HuBERT trained on about 200,000 hours improved music continuation and text-to-sound, at the cost of slightly less waveform detail. The open-source song model YuE uses a compact X-Codec; X-Codec 2 (2025) uses a single 65,536-entry codebook at 50 tokens per second with Wav2Vec2-BERT, powering the Llasa speech model (1B, 3B, 8B).

item.title: The World Goes Quiet When You Put Them On? How Noise Cancelling Headphones (ANC) Make Noise Disappear
item.description:
On the subway or a plane, you press the noise cancelling button and the rumble suddenly drops: your headphones are using sound to destroy sound. Little Pi first separates two kinds of quiet: passive isolation, where ear cups and ear tips block sound out, and active noise cancellation (ANC), where microphones and a chip create a sound that cancels the noise. The core idea: sound is air pressure going up and down; a microphone hears the noise, the chip instantly calculates an upside-down copy of the wave and plays it, so the peaks meet the troughs and they cancel out, which has to happen extremely fast. There are three microphone designs: feedforward on the outside, feedback near your ear checking what noise is left, and hybrid using both. Why can you still hear people talking? Steady low hums like engines and air conditioners are easiest to cancel, while fast-changing sounds like speech and typing are mostly blocked by passive isolation. History: in the 1930s German physicist Paul Lueg patented cancelling noise with an inverted wave; in 1978 Amar Bose, founder of Bose, was bothered by noise on a flight from Europe to the US and began sketching; a pilots' headset launched in 1989, and QuietComfort for passengers in 2000. Finally, transparency mode uses the outside microphones the other way to let outside sound in, so switch it on when walking or crossing the street; and in a quieter environment you don't need to turn your music way up.

item.title: Sound Flying Over Your Head? What Dolby Atmos and Spatial Audio Really Are
item.description:
At the movies a helicopter seems to fly right over your head, and now streaming services and headphones advertise Dolby Atmos and spatial audio. How is that different from old surround sound? From two-channel stereo to 5.1 and 7.1 surround (the point one is the subwoofer), the traditional approach assigns every sound to a fixed speaker during mixing. Dolby Atmos first adds height, with speakers on the ceiling. The bigger breakthrough is the sound object: background ambience stays in a fixed channel bed, while something like a passing bird is an object carrying coordinates, and at playback the system works out which speakers should play it based on how many speakers the room has and where they are. A film can carry up to 128 tracks and a theater can drive up to 64 speakers, so one mix adapts to large and small rooms alike. Pixar's Brave (2012) was the first film released in Dolby Atmos. No ceiling speakers at home? Soundbars bounce sound off the ceiling, and headphones simulate how your head and ears change sound to fool your brain, with head tracking keeping sounds in place when you turn. Apple Music launched spatial audio with Dolby Atmos in 2021, but mixers have to create a separate immersive mix; it isn't a button that turns old songs 3D.

item.title: How Does AI Understand Your Prompt? CLAP, the Matchmaker Between Text and Sound
item.description:
Type "lazy jazz piano on a rainy day" into an AI music site and you get music, but how does AI know which sound goes with which sentence? Meet CLAP (Contrastive Language-Audio Pretraining), inspired by OpenAI's 2021 image-text model CLIP. It works like two towers: a sound tower and a text tower turn a dog's bark and the words "a dog is barking" into 512 numbers each, placed on one shared map where matching meanings sit close together. Training is a matching game: a batch of sounds and descriptions forms a table, true pairs on the diagonal are pulled together and the rest pushed apart, with no hand labeling needed. The result is zero-shot classification: LAION-CLAP (2022), trained on about 630,000 pairs, scores 91.0% on the 50-class ESC-50 environmental sound test, above Microsoft CLAP's 82.6%. Generative AI uses it too: AudioLDM trains on sound coordinates and swaps in text coordinates to generate; Google's MusicLM uses the similar MuLan (44 million recordings); the first Stable Audio used its own CLAP, while Stable Audio Open switched to T5. The CLAP score is also a common way to grade whether AI output matches its prompt. Its weakness: a 2023 study found it can't really tell "one after another" from "at the same time"; it mostly notices keywords.

item.title: AI Draws a Photo Before It Speaks? Mel Spectrograms and Neural Vocoders
item.description:
Many AIs that talk or sing don't make sound directly: they first draw a "photo of sound," the mel spectrogram, and a neural vocoder turns it back into audio. A spectrogram puts time on the horizontal axis and pitch on the vertical, with brighter meaning louder; the mel scale (proposed in 1937, named after "melody") redraws the ruler the way ears hear, with fine slices for low sounds and coarse ones for high, often just 80 bands. But a spectrogram throws away phase, each wave's starting line. Griffin-Lim (1984) guesses it back over and over, and viral 2022 app Riffusion used it, giving a metallic flavor. Neural vocoders let AI learn to paint waveforms: DeepMind's WaveNet (2016) painted one point at a time, beautiful but slow; Kakao's HiFi-GAN (2020) uses a generative adversarial network, a forger painting waveforms from the mel spectrogram while teams of detectives judge real from fake, running 167.9x faster than real time on one V100 GPU; NVIDIA's BigVGAN (2022) is a universal vocoder that handles unseen singing and violins, and v2 supports 44.1 kHz. AudioLDM draws a mel spectrogram with diffusion and hands it to HiFi-GAN, while MusicGen takes the other road with the EnCodec decoder.

item.title: AI Stops Taking Detours! Flow Matching Walks a Straight Line
item.description:
Diffusion models wipe away noise one step at a time, and the path from noise back to sound is often twisty, so they need many steps and run slowly. Flow matching's idea is to just walk a straight line: take a piece of real sound and a handful of noise, connect them, pick any point on the line (the two mixed in proportion), and test the model on which way to go and how fast. The right answer is the real sound minus the noise, with no need to simulate the whole path. After lots of practice the model has an arrow map in its head (a vector field); to generate, start from noise and follow the arrows for a few steps. But millions of crossing lines still make the overall path bend a little: rectified flow (University of Texas, 2022) re-pairs with the trained model and trains again to straighten it, and Meta published the Flow Matching paper the same year. Speech AI adopted it first: Meta's Voicebox (2023) and the open-source F5-TTS (2024, led by Shanghai Jiao Tong University, 100,000 hours of multilingual speech, ten seconds of speech in about 1.5 seconds, with Sway Sampling spending more steps at the start). In music, open-source ACE-Step (2025) uses flow matching in latent space and makes a four-minute song in about 20 seconds on an A100; Stable Audio 3 (May 2026) builds on flow matching plus adversarial post-training to cut steps, taking under 2 seconds on an H200, with small and medium weights released.
References: Flow Matching for Generative Modeling (Lipman et al. 2022): https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.02747 Rectified Flow (Liu, Gong & Liu 2022): https://arxiv.org/abs/2209.03003 Voicebox (Le et al. 2023): https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.15687 F5-TTS (Chen et al. 2024): https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.06885 ACE-Step (2025): https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.00045 Stable Audio 3 (2026): https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.17991

item.title: Was This Song Made by AI? How Audio Watermarks and AI Detection Work
item.description:
AI songs sound more and more real: in July 2026 Deezer announced that more than half of the new songs uploaded each day are made by AI (about 90,000 a day at the June peak). There are two ways to tell AI audio apart. Watermarking slips an inaudible code into the sound at generation time and reads it back later with a decoder: very accurate, but it needs the AI company's cooperation. Detection looks for traces the AI left behind: it works on anyone's song but can guess wrong. Audio watermarks are trained with two neural networks together (an embedder and a detector), with deliberate attacks in between: MP3 conversion, noise, speed-ups, cuts. Meta's open-source AudioSeal (2024) scores every 1/16,000 of a second, so it can highlight the AI part of a spliced clip, and detects up to about 100x faster than WavMark. Google's SynthID sits in every sound made by Lyria; its checking site opened to everyone on October 7, but it only recognizes Google's and partners' codes, so Suno and Udio songs come back not detected. Not detected does not mean human-made. With no watermark, Deezer's team found that autoencoders leave evenly spaced little spikes on the spectrum when they scale data back up into sound, an AI fingerprint that reaches over 99% accuracy in several scenarios (ISMIR 2025 best paper). But pitch shifting, recompression, and new architectures make detection harder. AI songs are half the uploads yet only 1-3% of plays, and about 85% of those plays are fraudulent and go unpaid.

item.title: Why Do Pop Vocals Sound So Perfectly in Tune? How Auto-Tune Works
item.description:
Why does every note in pop vocals sound so perfect, and where does that jumpy robot voice come from? Auto-Tune's inventor, Andy Hildebrand, was an Exxon engineer who analyzed seismic waves to find oil. As the story goes, a friend at dinner joked that he should build a box to make her sing in tune; he realized the same math could analyze the voice, and Auto-Tune arrived in 1997. It works in three steps: autocorrelation (comparing the waveform with a shifted copy of itself until it lines up after exactly one cycle) finds how high you're singing; it picks the nearest note the song uses; then it pushes only the pitch there, keeping your timing and lyrics. The key knob, retune speed, sounds natural when slow; set to zero, the pitch snaps instantly, creating the robot voice of Cher's 1998 hit Believe (the producers reportedly first claimed it was a vocoder). Why no chipmunk effect? Good pitch correction keeps the formants, the resonances shaped by your throat and mouth. Melodyne goes further, drawing each note as a draggable blob. T-Pain made the robot voice his signature, Jay-Z released D.O.A. (Death of Auto-Tune) in 2009, yet it never went away: gentle correction is now standard in recording, and the obvious robot voice is an effect, like guitar distortion.

item.title: Writing Down Every Note from a Recording? How AI Music Transcription Works: Basic Pitch and MT3
item.description:
Writing down every note you hear is called transcription; it used to take a trained ear, and now AI can do it. A single voice is easy (like Auto-Tune's pitch tracking in episode 57), but in a chord the overtones pile up, so AI may mistake an overtone for a note or guess the wrong octave, and it must also know when each note starts and ends. Most transcription AIs draw the sound as a spectrogram (episode 53) and then draw a piano roll, one bar per note. Google's Onsets and Frames (2018) trains two detectors at once, one for note starts and one for whether a note is still sounding, which greatly improved piano transcription. Spotify's open-source Basic Pitch (2022) is light and instrument-agnostic: voice, guitar, piano; it runs on a laptop or in the browser and captures slides and vibrato, though it works best on one source at a time. Google Magenta's MT3 treats transcription as translation: spectrogram in, a stream of MIDI-like tokens out (instrument, time, note on/off), written one by one like the word chain from episode 37, transcribing many instruments at once and labeling who played each note. But MIDI is not yet a score: aligning to beats, choosing F sharp or G flat, splitting voices and adding markings are still hurdles ahead.

item.title: How Does AI "Read" Music? Cutting Music into Words: Symbolic Tokens, REMI, ABC Notation and NotaGen
item.description:
MusicGen generates sound directly, but another camp of music AI writes a score first. Language models read words, so what words should music be cut into? Audio tokens (episode 36) run about 200 per second and record the sound itself; symbolic tokens record what to play: which note, which beat, how long, about a dozen per bar, easy to edit and playable on any instrument, but with no timbre. Approach one: Google Magenta (2018) wrote MIDI events (press, wait, release), great for real performances, but time is in seconds, so AI can't find the beat. Approach two: REMI from Yi-Hsuan Yang's team in Taiwan (Pop Music Transformer, 2020) adds bar and position words, sixteen slots per bar like graph paper, plus pitch, velocity and duration, giving much steadier rhythm. Approach three: ABC notation, a plain-text notation Chris Walshaw formalized in 1993 for folk tunes, which language models read naturally. NotaGen (2025), led by the Central Conservatory of Music in Beijing, pretrains on about 1.6 million ABC scores, fine-tunes on about 9,000 classical pieces, and is prompted with period, composer and instrumentation; CLaMP-DPO then uses the CLaMP model as a judge so it learns more from outputs that resemble real scores, with no human grading, and it beat other models in blind tests.
References: This Time with Feeling (Oore et al. 2018): https://arxiv.org/abs/1808.03715 Pop Music Transformer / REMI (Huang & Yang 2020): https://arxiv.org/abs/2002.00212 MidiTok tokenizations: https://miditok.readthedocs.io/en/latest/tokenizations.html ABC notation - Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ABC_notation A brief history of abc: https://abcnotation.com/history NotaGen (Wang et al., IJCAI 2025): https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.18008

item.title: Singing into a Violin? Letting AI Turn the Synth Knobs: DDSP, Tone Transfer and DDSP-VST
item.description:
Hum into a microphone and out comes a violin? Google Magenta's DDSP (Differentiable Digital Signal Processing, ICLR 2020) doesn't make the AI draw waveforms from scratch; it lets the AI turn a synthesizer's knobs. Neural vocoders (episode 53) draw tens of thousands of points per second and need big models and lots of data. DDSP first extracts pitch with CREPE and loudness, the two lines describing what is played, then hands them to an AI that has only heard the violin, which decides how to turn the knobs, so a voice or a flute becomes a violin. The synthesizer has three parts: harmonics (dozens of sine waves, additive synthesis, whose levels set the timbre), filtered noise (breath, bow scratch), and reverb (the room). Differentiable means the effect of every tiny knob turn can be calculated, so training compares spectra and traces back which way to turn each knob. The models are several times smaller than similar neural synthesizers, each official example trained on under thirteen minutes of audio, and pitch and loudness can be edited separately; the limit is one note at a time. Magenta launched the Tone Transfer web app in October 2020 (flute, saxophone, trumpet, violin) and the free DDSP-VST plugin in 2022; ten to twenty minutes of single-note playing can train your own timbre model.

item.title: Turning Drums into Voices Live? AI Timbre Transfer on a Laptop: IRCAM RAVE, nn~ and Neutone
item.description:
Play some drums and out comes something like a human voice? In 2021, Antoine Caillon and Philippe Esling at IRCAM introduced RAVE (Realtime Audio Variational autoEncoder). Where DDSP handles one note at a time, RAVE takes drums, noise and chords. Its backbone is the autoencoder from episode 45: the encoder squeezes each slice of sound into a few numbers, and a decoder that has only heard voices answers everything in a voice, keeping the drum rhythm while swapping the timbre. Training has two stages: first learn to compress and restore (matching spectra, but a bit blurry), then freeze the encoder and fine-tune adversarially with a judge, the same trick as the neural vocoders in episode 53. A multi-band decomposition splits sound into 16 bands computed at once, so 48 kHz audio runs about 20 times faster than real time on an ordinary laptop CPU (the authors' own test). On stage, nn~ loads models in Max/MSP and Pure Data (export in streaming mode to avoid clicks), Qosmo's Neutone plugin runs RAVE models in a DAW, and a lightweight version even runs on a Raspberry Pi. You can also push the latent numbers directly to make new sounds, or let it generate with no input. Finally, DDSP (one note, easy control) vs RAVE (any sound, but no clear pitch knob).

item.title: Songs the Singer Never Sang? AI Singing Synthesis and AI Covers: DiffSinger and RVC
item.description:
AI covers online sound just like real singers performing songs they never sang. There are two roads for AI singing: singing voice synthesis creates a voice from lyrics, notes and durations, while singing voice conversion keeps an existing recording's melody and lyrics but swaps the voice. Yamaha's VOCALOID (2004) stitched together syllables recorded by a real singer, the way Hatsune Miku sings, but the seams sound robotic; today neural networks paint the whole sound directly. DiffSinger (AAAI 2022) uses the diffusion models from episode 38 with a shortcut called shallow diffusion: a simple model draws a blurry rough draft, a little noise is added, and cleaning starts from the middle, so it takes fewer steps and gives clearer detail; the mel spectrogram then goes to a vocoder (episode 53). The community OpenVPI version works with the free OpenUtau editor. RVC (Retrieval-based Voice Conversion, viral in 2023) separates what is sung from who sings it: HuBERT (episode 49) captures the words, RMVPE captures pitch, and a retrieval step blends in the most similar snippets from the target singer's recordings before a decoder sings in the new voice; about ten minutes of clean vocals can train a model. An AI cover takes three steps: source separation (episode 35), RVC, and mixing back with the accompaniment. Finally, whose voice is it? In 2023 Heart on My Sleeve imitated Drake and The Weeknd and was taken down; Holly Herndon launched Holly+ in 2021, and Grimes launched Elf.Tech in 2023 with a fifty-fifty royalty split. Always get permission before using someone else's voice.

item.title: Hear a Mosquito with Your Eyes Closed? How Two Ears Find Direction | Spatial Sound Series 1
item.description:
The first episode of the Spatial Sound Series! A mosquito buzzes by your ear at night, and you know which side it's on without opening your eyes. How? Your two ears work like two microphones, and the brain compares them. First, the time difference: a sound from the left reaches the left ear first; with ears only a little more than ten centimeters apart, the biggest gap is about 0.6 to 0.7 milliseconds, yet the brain can detect around a hundred-thousandth of a second. Second, the loudness difference: the head casts an acoustic shadow that blocks short high-frequency waves, while long low-frequency waves bend around it. Lord Rayleigh's duplex theory (1907) says low sounds are located mainly by time and high sounds mainly by loudness, with the dividing line around 1500 hertz (he also won the Nobel Prize in Physics for discovering argon). That's why you can hardly tell where a subwoofer sits, though the room still shapes how full the bass sounds. The loophole: front-left and back-left give almost the same differences. These confusable positions form an ice-cream-cone shape called the cone of confusion; turning your head helps (Wallach, 1940), and the outer ear is another secret weapon. Finally, the barn owl, whose ear openings sit at different heights so it can hear up and down too.

item.title: How Loud Is Too Loud for Headphones? The 60/60 Rule and WHO Safe Listening
item.description:
Turning up your headphones on a noisy train and leaving with ringing ears? Loudness is measured in decibels: a quiet library is about 30, normal conversation about 60, a noisy train or busy road about 80, and the front rows of a concert can exceed 110. Every 10 more decibels means ten times the energy and sounds roughly twice as loud. The World Health Organization recommends that adults listen at up to 80 decibels for a total of 40 hours a week (75 decibels for children), and every 3 more decibels halves the safe time: 10 hours at 86 decibels, just 2.5 hours at 92. Hair cells in the cochlea, like tiny blades of grass, turn vibrations into nerve signals; too much loud sound damages them, and human hair cells don't grow back. Muffled or ringing ears are a warning sign. WHO estimates about half of people aged 12 to 35 are at risk, and a 2022 BMJ Global Health study estimated 0.67 to 1.35 billion young people have unsafe listening habits. Three tips: the 60/60 rule, your phone's headphone level alerts (iPhone uses 80 decibels for 40 hours over 7 days), and noise-cancelling headphones in loud places (episode 50).

item.title: Why Is Vinyl Back in the Streaming Era? How Records Make Sound, and Do They Sound Better?
item.description:
We can stream over a hundred million songs, yet people line up for vinyl. A record is one long spiral groove whose walls are cut in the shape of the sound wave; the needle wiggles along it and the cartridge turns that motion into an electrical signal. History: Edison's tin-foil cylinder phonograph (1877), Emile Berliner's flat disc (1887), Columbia's long-playing record with about 20 minutes per side (1948), and the CD (1982), after which vinyl faded. In 2008, independent US record stores launched Record Store Day; in 2022, vinyl outsold CDs by units in the US for the first time since 1987; in 2024 the US sold about 44 million vinyl records versus 33 million CDs, with vinyl revenue around 1.4 billion dollars, the highest since 1984. Does vinyl sound better? On specs, CDs have less noise and more dynamic range; vinyl has crackles and inner-groove distortion. Its warmth partly comes from subtle distortion and from separate vinyl masters (bass kept centered so the needle stays in the groove, sometimes less loudness compression). It sounds different, not better. Big covers, the ritual of playing a record, and supporting artists add to the appeal; a 2023 Luminate survey found only about half of recent US vinyl buyers said they owned a record player.

item.title: How Does Sound Get Behind Your Head in Headphones? The Pinna, HRTF and Dummy Heads | Spatial Sound Series 2
item.description:
Part two of the spatial sound series! How can footsteps come from behind you in headphones? Last time, our two ears used time and level differences to tell left from right, but front-back and up-down are easy to confuse. Today's hero is the pinna: its folds act as a direction filter, carving notches into certain frequencies, and the notch moves depending on whether sound comes from above, in front or below. The head's shadow, the pinna's notches and reflections from the shoulders and body together make up the head-related transfer function (HRTF), a fingerprint book with left- and right-ear fingerprints for every direction. Everyone's ears differ: in 1998, a Dutch team (Hofman et al.) fitted silicone molds into listeners' ears; elevation judgments collapsed, the brain relearned within several weeks, and the original ears worked immediately once the molds came out. The KEMAR dummy head, introduced by Knowles in 1972, has microphones in its ears; surrounded by speakers, it records each direction's fingerprint, and in 1994 the MIT Media Lab released measurements for over 700 directions for free. Two approaches: dummy-head recording on location (already at the 1881 Paris electricity exhibition, two telephone lines sent opera sound separately to each ear), or a binaural panner that applies a direction's HRTF to a mono sound; with head tracking, sounds stay put when you turn. Using someone else's HRTF causes front-back reversals and in-head sound (Wenzel et al., 1993), which is why some phones scan your ears to personalize it.

item.title: How Far Away Is That Sound? Four Clues Your Ears Use to Judge Distance | Spatial Sound Series 3
item.description:
Part three of the spatial sound series! With your eyes closed, you still know whether the person calling you is right beside you or down the hall. Your ears have no ruler, so they rely on several clues. Clue one is loudness: sound spreads out in all directions, and outdoors it drops about 6 dB every time the distance doubles. But loudness can lie: a whisper in your ear and a shout from across a sports field may arrive equally loud, and your brain uses what it knows about how loud a sound normally is, so unfamiliar sounds are hard to judge. Clue two is the ratio of direct sound to reverberation: as you move away, the direct sound weakens while the reverberation stays roughly constant in the room, so close sounds feel dry and distant ones feel wet. In 1975, Mershon and King found that listeners judged distance more accurately in a reverberant room than in an anechoic chamber, so reverberation is your ears' measuring tape. Clue three is air absorption: about 100 meters away, very high frequencies lose almost 10 dB while lows barely change, which is why nearby thunder cracks and distant thunder rumbles. Clue four is the near field: within one meter, the head's shadow becomes so strong that even low frequencies differ between the ears (Brungart and Rabinowitz, 1999), which is how binaural whisper videos work. Finally, how mixing engineers push sounds back (quieter, more reverb, fewer highs) or pull them close, and how a little room reverb keeps headphone sound from feeling stuck inside your head.

item.title: Who Scores AI Music? Fréchet Audio Distance (FAD) Explained
item.description:
AI can generate ten thousand songs overnight, but nobody can listen to them all, so researchers need an automatic ruler. This episode explains FAD, the Fréchet Audio Distance, the score you see most often in AI music papers. Generated songs have no reference answer to compare against point by point, so in 2019 Kilgour and colleagues at Google proposed FAD, originally for evaluating music enhancement. It works in three steps: an AI model trained on lots of sounds (originally VGGish) acts as the ears and turns each song into a list of numbers, a point in space; the real-music and AI-music point clouds are each summarized by a center and a spread, like an ellipse; and FAD combines the distance between the centers with the difference in shape. Lower is better, and models like MusicLM and MusicGen use it to compare themselves. FAD has traps: fewer songs push the score up, the wrong embedding model misses high-frequency detail, a poor reference playlist bends the ruler, and it ignores whether songs follow the text prompt (that's what the CLAP score is for). Finally, the improvements: Microsoft's 2023 fadtk extrapolates to infinitely many songs (FAD-infinity), recommends music-aware embeddings and scores each song individually, and 2025's KAD drops the ellipse assumption and stabilizes with fewer songs.
References: Kilgour et al. 2019 (Interspeech): https://www.isca-archive.org/interspeech_2019/kilgour19_interspeech.html Gui et al., Adapting Frechet Audio Distance for Generative Music Evaluation: https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.01616 microsoft/fadtk: https://github.com/microsoft/fadtk KAD: No More FAD!: https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.15602

item.title: Sound Bounces Everywhere, So How Do We Still Hear Direction? The Precedence (Haas) Effect | Spatial Sound Series 4
item.description:
Part four of the spatial sound series! At an indoor concert, the singer's voice bounces off walls and ceiling and reaches you from every direction, yet with your eyes closed you still know the singer is center stage. The key is timing: the direct sound takes the shortest path and arrives first, while reflections take a detour and arrive later (sound travels about 34 centimeters per millisecond), usually a few to a few tens of milliseconds behind. For direction, the brain trusts only the first arrival: two identical sounds close together are heard as one, located at the first one. Wallach and colleagues named this the precedence effect in 1949. Under one millisecond, the two sounds merge into an image in between (how a stereo vocal sits between two speakers); from about 1 to 30 milliseconds is the precedence zone; any later and you hear an echo, and short clicks like hand claps reveal echoes sooner than speech. In his doctoral thesis, Helmut Haas found that a sound arriving 10 to 30 milliseconds later can be about 10 dB louder and still lose the direction contest, which is why it's also called the Haas effect. Application one: delay speakers in big venues are set to arrive a little over ten milliseconds after the stage sound, so they add level while the sound still seems to come from the stage. Application two: the Haas widening trick in mixing, copying a track to left and right and delaying one side, which sounds wide and thick but can cause comb filtering on a single phone speaker, so check in mono. Finally, reflections aren't thrown away: direction comes from the first arrival, while room size, distance and fullness come from the reflections.

item.title: Headphones vs. Speakers: Crosstalk, Crosstalk Cancellation, and the Sweet Spot | Spatial Sound Series 5
item.description:
Part five of the spatial sound series! The same song can feel like it's inside your head on headphones but out in the room on speakers. Why? With headphones, each channel goes only into its own ear. With speakers, each speaker's sound also wraps around your head into the other ear: that's crosstalk. Crosstalk isn't always bad. Alan Blumlein's 1931 stereo invention relies on it: level differences between two speakers mix at the ears and become interaural time differences at low frequencies. But binaural (dummy head) recordings capture exactly what each ear hears, so on speakers, crosstalk scrambles the cues and everything collapses between the speakers. The fix is crosstalk cancellation: the other speaker sends a polarity-flipped, precisely timed copy that cancels the leak at the ear. Bishnu Atal and Manfred Schroeder developed it at Bell Labs in the 1960s; it later became known as transaural. The costs: a tiny sweet spot, since moving a few centimeters breaks high-frequency cancellation (some systems track your head with a camera, and laptop and soundbar virtual surround use a similar idea), and at certain pitches the system must push hard to compensate, stressing the speakers and changing timbre, a trade-off between accurate direction and natural tone. Ordinary stereo has a sweet spot too: sit at the corner of an equilateral triangle, because if you sit off-center, the nearer speaker arrives first and the precedence effect pulls the vocal toward it. Finally, we compare the strengths of headphones and speakers.

item.title: Why Do You Hear Your Own Echo in Video Calls? And Where Does That Piercing Feedback Beep Come From?
item.description:
Ever hear your own voice come back a beat late in an online meeting, or a shrill beep that makes everyone cover their ears? The echo path: your voice travels to the other person's computer, plays from their speakers, gets picked up by their microphone, and comes back to you. The internet round trip takes a few hundred milliseconds, so you hear yourself late, and it's usually the other side's setup causing it. With that much delay, the brain hears a second sound (recall the precedence effect), and hearing yourself delayed can even make people stutter. Most calls have no echo thanks to echo cancellation: the computer knows what its speakers played, estimates how it will sound after reaching the microphone, and subtracts it, continuously learning the room. It was developed at Bell Labs in the 1960s for overseas phone calls. It slips up when speakers are too loud and distort, when both sides talk at once, or when you move the laptop, and sometimes it suppresses too hard and makes you sound choppy. Feedback is a loop: microphone, amplifier, speaker, back into the microphone; if a pitch grows a little each time around, it snowballs. Two computers in the same room with mics and speakers on is the classic cause, and echo cancellation can't help. item.title: Great Recordings on Your Phone: Get Closer, Pick the Right Room, and Don't Clip | Phone Recording Tips
item.description:
Phone recordings of talking, singing, or playing that sound hollow, distant, and noisy? No need for new gear yet; a few habits make a big difference. Tip one, get closer: doubling the distance drops your voice about 6 dB while room echo and noise stay the same; for speech, keep the phone a hand's length to an arm's length away, but not so close that plosives pop. Tip two, find the microphone: there are holes at the bottom, top, and next to the rear camera, so keep fingers and cases off them. Tip three, choose the room: bathrooms and empty rooms are echoey, while curtains, sofas, and rugs soak up reflections; a closet full of clothes is a podcaster's secret weapon. Turn off fans, air conditioning, and range hoods. Tip four, don't clip: if it's too loud, the waveform gets cut flat and it's almost impossible to fix later, so test-record the loudest part; for drums, piano, or high singing, move the phone farther away, and some apps let you turn off automatic level control. Tip five, beware of wind: shield the phone with your body or a wall, or use a fuzzy windscreen (the "dead cat"). Tip six, settings and placement: Do Not Disturb or airplane mode, the highest audio quality setting, and a steady surface instead of your hand. Finally, listen back on headphones, and consider a clip-on lavalier mic.
